transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Good morning, Mr. Okafor. I wanted to come by and speak with you about the chest X-ray we did yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Good morning. I was actually wondering about that. I haven't heard the results yet. Was everything alright?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm afraid there was a mistake. The portable X-ray was performed with you positioned incorrectly, which meant the image we got was of insufficient diagnostic quality. It wasn't a clear picture, but the report mistakenly labeled it as normal without realizing the image was poor.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, so you're saying the image wasn't actually usable?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct. The angle of the plate didn't capture the area we needed to see, so the result we relied on was inaccurate. Does that make sense so far?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It does, but I'm confused. If the quality was that bad, how did the doctor reading it just say it was normal? That seems like a pretty big oversight.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I agree. It was a failure in our process. I apologize for this error; our team is responsible for this mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm just... I've been lying here thinking everything was fine based on that report. Now I'm wondering what else might have been missed. It's a bit unsettling.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. But look, the important thing is that we've identified it now and we can fix it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I suppose, but it makes me feel like I can't trust the—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have to go through the other patients' charts quickly, so I want to make sure we get to the solution here. To make sure I've explained the technical part clearly, do you understand why the first image didn't work?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, you said the positioning was wrong. But I'm more concerned about the fact that I was told I was fine when you didn't actually know if I was.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. But like I said, I understand. Now, we just need to get a new image.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is there any risk that the delay in getting a correct image has changed my treatment or the outcome?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We don't believe so, but we need to verify it. I'm going to order a repeat X-ray.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When exactly is that happening? And who is ensuring that the positioning is correct this time? I don't want to go through this again.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll get someone down here soon. Probably sometime today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Soon isn't a time. Is it within the hour? And will the attending physician be reviewing the quality of the image before the report is signed off?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It should be this afternoon. Let's just wrap this up so we can get the technician in here. I'll put the order in the system now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel like you're rushing me. I'm asking legitimate questions about my care.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm just trying to be efficient for your sake. We'll just get the new scan and then we'll see where we stand.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('go through the other patients' charts quickly', 'wrap this up', 'trying to be efficient') and interrupts the patient's expression of distrust.

E.justification: Error named in first turn, used lay language, checked comprehension twice ('Does that make sense so far?', 'do you understand why...'), and avoided false reassurance.

A.justification: Directly apologized ('I apologize for this error'), explicitly took team responsibility, and did not deflect when the patient questioned the oversight.

R.justification: Resident used only generic validation ('I understand', 'I hear you') and consistently redirected emotional bids back to the factual plan.

T.justification: Resident provided a vague next step (repeat X-ray) with a vague timeline ('soon', 'this afternoon') and no patient role or prevention strategy.
